item.title: CNMI governor seeks revenue sharing, safeguards in seabed mining proposal
item.description: Gov. David M. Apatang said the Commonwealth supports national efforts to secure critical mineral supplies but urged federal officials to address a wide range of environmental, economic and cultural concerns before advancing a proposed offshore mineral lease sale near the Northern Mariana Islands. In comments submitted Oct. 16 to the U.S. Dept. of the Interior and its Marine Minerals Administration
item.content:encoded:
Gov. David M. Apatang said the Commonwealth supports national efforts to secure critical mineral supplies but urged federal officials to address a wide range of environmental, economic and cultural concerns before advancing a proposed offshore mineral lease sale near the Northern Mariana Islands.

In comments submitted Oct. 16 to the U.S. Dept. of the Interior and its Marine Minerals Administration, Apatang said he recognizes and supports President Donald Trump's goal of reducing U.S. dependence on foreign sources of critical minerals used in technology, clean energy, transportation, health care and defense industries. However, he said national supply-chain objectives should not outweigh potential impacts on CNMI residents and the marine environment.

"The CNMI cannot evaluate the proposed lease sale solely on the basis of national mineral supply chain security objectives and dominance," Apatang wrote, adding that any decision should balance national interests with the well-being of CNMI residents and marine ecosystems.

The governor's comments were submitted in response to the proposed leasing notice for Pacific Minerals Lease Sale 2, or PACM-2, which would make portions of the Outer Continental Shelf around the CNMI available for critical mineral exploration and development.

Apatang noted that more than 65,000 public comments were submitted during an earlier federal information-gathering process and said all should be considered, particularly those expressing concerns about potential environmental harm from deep-sea mining. He said residents have voiced strong opposition to offshore mining and emphasized the longstanding cultural and personal connection indigenous island communities have with the ocean.

The governor also encouraged federal officials to pause the leasing process until two pending federal court cases in Hawaii have been resolved, arguing that proceeding before judicial review is completed could prove inefficient and costly.

In an 11-page letter, Apatang outlined numerous questions and recommendations for federal officials, including whether the CNMI would receive a share of lease revenues and what economic benefits would flow to the Commonwealth if mining activities move forward. He also called for enforceable commitments on local hiring, procurement, workforce development, and infrastructure investments.

The governor further requested additional environmental baseline studies addressing deep-sea coral communities, seamount ecosystems, fisheries, marine mammals, sediment plumes, underwater noise and other potential impacts. He proposed creating a CNMI Marine Minerals Environmental Monitoring Program funded by leaseholders.

Among other recommendations, Apatang sought fisheries compensation mechanisms, protections for cultural and traditional resources, stronger financial assurance requirements, emergency-response funding, safeguards against excessive concentration of lease ownership and restrictions on foreign control of strategically important mineral resources.

He also asked federal officials to clarify how offshore mineral activities would be coordinated with military operations in the Mariana Islands Range Complex and requested a formal framework for continued CNMI participation in future review and permitting processes.

Apatang said the CNMI remains willing to work with federal agencies to identify what he described as a responsible path forward, but stressed that residents should not bear disproportionate environmental, economic or infrastructure-related costs associated with offshore mineral development. He acknowledged that many residents favor a more direct alternative.

"The alternative, as voiced by many CNMI residents, is no mining at all," Apatang wrote

item.title: Bureau of Women’s Affairs is accepting domestic violence grant applications
item.description: The Guam Bureau of Women’s Affairs is accepting proposals from qualified organizations seeking federal funding for programs addressing domestic violence, dating violence, sexual assault, and stalking. The funding is available through the U.S. Department of Justice’s Services, Training, Officers and Prosecutors (STOP) Violence Against Women Formula Grant Program. Guam was awarded nearly $668,000 un
item.content:encoded:
The Guam Bureau of Women’s Affairs is accepting proposals from qualified organizations seeking federal funding for programs addressing domestic violence, dating violence, sexual assault, and stalking.

The funding is available through the U.S. Department of Justice’s Services, Training, Officers and Prosecutors (STOP) Violence Against Women Formula Grant Program. Guam was awarded nearly $668,000 under the program in fiscal year 2024.

Eligible applicants include local criminal justice agencies, such as law enforcement agencies, prosecutors, and courts, 501(c)(3) nonprofit victim-service organizations, including faith-based and community-based organizations, and local violence or sexual assault coalitions.

Organizations must demonstrate expertise in addressing domestic violence, dating violence, sexual assault, and stalking. Applicants proposing new projects must also explain the need for their proposed program, identify gaps in existing services, and show how their work would complement services already available in the community.

Grant funding may support existing programs or new initiatives that meet program guidelines. Eligible projects include victim services and efforts to strengthen law enforcement and justice system responses to violence against women.

Organizations proposing new projects must submit completed applications by 4 p.m. Nov. 20. Existing grant recipients seeking continued funding must also complete requirements to maintain their funding.

For application materials, submission requirements, or questions, contact the Bureau of Women’s Affairs at (671) 475-9178 or email gcofpo@guam.gov .

item.title: Julia Birn’s first solo exhibition explores chronic illness through art

item.content:encoded:
The Guam Museum Café Gallery will host “ Chewing on Static ,” the first solo exhibition by multidisciplinary artist and graphic designer Julia Birn, with the opening reception from 10 a.m. to 2 p.m. Oct. 24.

Birn, a recent graduate of the Savannah College of Art and Design, lives with hypermobile Ehlers-Danlos syndrome and dysautonomia, a broad umbrella term for any malfunction of the autonomic nervous system, which controls automatic body functions like heart rate and blood pressure. Her main diagnosis also includes postural orthostatic tachycardia syndrome, or POTS, a specific, common type of dysautonomia defined by an abnormal jump in heart rate. Her experiences with chronic illness inform her artwork and the exhibit, which explores uncertainty through abstraction, fragmentation, and limited color palettes.

Birn said discussing chronic illness can help people better understand the conditions of those who live with chronic illness and raise awareness.

“I’m very open to talking about what chronic illnesses I have because talking about it is how we learn more about it,” Birn said. “We learn how people deal with it. It helps get awareness to the situations and the illnesses.”

She also hopes the exhibition encourages people to consider art as a way to express experiences, like she does, beyond happiness and positive moments.

“Because art is supposed to be expressive. It doesn’t need to focus on just the happy moments or fun times,” Birn said. “And I think pushing that perspective will really expand people’s knowledge of art and how they feel towards it, and I feel like that’s needed here.”

The exhibit will remain on view through Dec. 1.

The Guam Museum is open Tuesday through Friday from 9 a.m. to 4 p.m. and Saturdays from 10 a.m. to 2 p.m.

item.title: AIPAC halts endorsements and direct contributions to candidates
item.description: The pro-Israel political organization AIPAC, or the American Israel Public Affairs Committee, announced on Wednesday that it will no longer issue endorsements, make direct PAC contributions or earmark funds for candidates. A longtime influential lobbying group, AIPAC started its direct political involvement five years ago. Since then, particularly this midterm election cycle, AIPAC has been met wi
item.content:encoded:
The pro-Israel political organization AIPAC, or the American Israel Public Affairs Committee, announced on Wednesday that it will no longer issue endorsements, make direct PAC contributions or earmark funds for candidates.

A longtime influential lobbying group, AIPAC started its direct political involvement five years ago. Since then, particularly this midterm election cycle, AIPAC has been met with mounting resistance. The group has faced criticism over its stances on various issues, including the wars in Gaza and Iran.

Candidates endorsed by AIPAC have also faced tough opposition from both the political right and the political left for accepting the organization's support and financial contributions as public opinion on the U.S. relationship with Israel has shifted. In order to tame the criticism, some AIPAC-endorsed candidates said they won't accept any money from the organization.

AIPAC first announced the changes in a letter to members, stating "the challenges we are confronting will continue to grow in the years ahead." In the letter, AIPAC said it wouldn't stop funneling money to candidates that align with the group's mission by mobilizing individual donors.

"We will prioritize increasing direct, organized contributions from individual Americans to candidates—expanding upon our current efforts—and maximizing the emerging political fundraising tools," the letter said.

The letter added that the 2028 cycle will "demand an even stronger commitment by our activists to pro-Israel politics." As a result, the group plans to increase support "for the Republicans and Democrats who are advancing policies that strengthen America's alliance with Israel and standing up against anti-Israel legislation."

In a statement to NPR, AIPAC spokesperson Deryn Sousa said the group's mission and strategy remains the same despite the changes.

"Our goal is to build support for the U.S.-Israel relationship. AIPAC members gave more than $90 million directly to candidates this cycle, and that organized, direct giving from our members will continue and increase."

AIPAC contributed nearly $25 million to candidates and political committees in 2026 through Sept. 30, according to FEC filings. Its affiliated super PAC United Democracy Project contributed $13 million to candidates and political committees and spent an additional $53.5 million in independent expenditures.

AIPAC confirmed with NPR that its affiliated super PAC, United Democracy Project, will continue to operate and will be able to raise an unlimited amount of money. It has spent heavily to support pro-Israel candidates, and oppose those who criticize Israel.

In recent days, several of the super PAC's individual independent expenditures are being used to campaign against Abdul El-Sayed, the Democratic nominee for U.S. Senate in Michigan.

AIPAC also spent heavily to campaign against El-Sayed in the primary, backing his opponent, Rep. Haley Stevens. The Michigan Senate contest is just one of the high-profile races where AIPAC has spent in favor of a pro-Israel politician or in opposition to someone the organization sees as less favorable to Israel.

item.title: The Justice Department begins notifying counties where it wants to monitor elections
item.description: The Department of Justice this week began notifying the counties it wants to monitor on Election Day, NPR has learned. Counties in Colorado, Florida, Minnesota, Texas and Washington have received notifications from the Justice Department so far, but the list seems to be growing in real time.
item.content:encoded:
The Department of Justice this week began notifying the counties it wants to monitor on Election Day, NPR has learned.

Counties in Colorado, Florida, Minnesota, Texas and Washington have received notifications from the Justice Department so far, but the list seems to be growing in real time.

The department has long deployed monitors to ensure compliance with voting laws, but the Trump administration's unprecedented steps to try to wrestle control over elections from local and state governments have led to new concerns about DOJ monitoring this year. And already this week, at least one county official is raising questions about why his locality is on the DOJ's list.

Last month, Harmeet Dhillon, the head of the Justice Department's Civil Rights Division, said the department planned to send 1,000 observers nationwide, in what she termed "the largest monitoring effort" in DOJ history.

And even as counties are being notified, it's unclear which jurisdictions or how many the department plans to monitor this November. A DOJ spokesperson, Kiersten Pels, told NPR those details will be shared "closer to the election."

The Justice Department routinely observes elections. The department under President Biden monitored 64 jurisdictions in 24 states on Election Day in the last midterm year, 2022.

But to many local officials and experts, this year is different.

President Trump continues to falsely maintain that he won the 2020 election and that election fraud is more widespread than it has ever been proven to be. Experts worry federal law enforcement could potentially use those false claims — or others generated this year — as pretext to try to seize ballots during the counting period, or interfere in the process in some other way.

Most states reported no incidents with Justice Department monitors during primary elections earlier this year, but in Wyoming, the state's Republican governor expressed concern about "aggressive" and "irregular" behavior by monitors for the state's August primary. And the Republican county clerk of Laramie County told NBC News that the conduct of the monitors "showed complete disregard for our state laws and administration of our elections."

The Department of Justice disputes that characterization.

"We disagree with the public framing that the two monitors we sent were 'aggressive' or did anything improper," Pels said, adding that Dhillon had a meeting with the Wyoming officials after the fact.

In previous election cycles, state officials in the states where monitors were assigned were notified at the same time as the counties. This year, that did not happen initially, according to officials in three states who spoke to NPR anonymously because they weren't authorized to speak to the press. So states have been scrambling since the notifications began going out Tuesday to figure out where the DOJ plans to be.

After NPR asked the DOJ why states had not been notified, multiple state officials told NPR they then received notification from the department.

One of the counties that received a notification is Adams County, Colo.

The clerk there, Democrat Josh Zygielbaum, told NPR he wasn't shocked the DOJ selected his county to observe, as Adams County includes part of the state's 8th Congressional District, a toss-up district that could determine party control of the House of Representatives next year.

Zygielbaum was surprised however that the DOJ reached out only to him, and not the Republican clerk in neighboring Weld County, which also houses a sizable portion of that same congressional district.

"My initial thought is that it's politically motivated, and that this is potentially an intimidation technique," Zygielbaum said. "Although I like to assume the best in people, the administration really has shown its disdain for elections, particularly in states and counties where mail ballots exist."

Pels, of the DOJ, said the department prioritizes places with competitive elections, and would monitor Adams County because it is covered by Section 203 of the Voting Rights Act, which requires voters be given access to election materials in the language they speak. Weld County is not covered under that provision.

That explanation didn't fully comfort Zygielbaum.

"The fact that we're covered by Section 203 means we have a higher portion of Spanish-speaking voters who have a right to vote," Zygielbaum said. "It still doesn't put me at ease that it's not a targeted visit."

NPR reported in September that Trump administration officials assigned to noncitizen voting issues last year circulated a list of counties covered by Section 203, along with a DOJ criminal checklist outlining requirements for prosecution of voter-related charges.

Colorado state officials say they are considering how to respond to the DOJ's request, considering Colorado election rules say observers need to have permission from the secretary of state's office, unless they are ordered to observe by a court.

"We are considering these requests in collaboration with the Attorney General's Office," said Jack Todd, a spokesperson for the Colorado secretary of state's office.

Zygielbaum says his election processes won't change either way. He has, however, already requested a staffer from the state come to Adams County on Election Day just to keep an eye on the federal monitors if they do come.

"I have lots of questions about why they're there and what their ultimate intent is," he said.

NPR has confirmed the DOJ has also sent monitor notifications to seven counties in Texas, King County, Wash., Miami-Dade County, Fla., and Hennepin and Ramsey counties in Minnesota.

The DOJ requested to send monitors to the same Minnesota counties during the state's primary in August, but monitors were denied close access to polling locations. A spokesperson for the Minnesota secretary of state's office said it was too soon to know whether a different decision would be made for this fall's general election.

In 2024, Texas similarly blocked the Biden-era DOJ from election monitoring. Ken Paxton, the state attorney general and current Republican nominee for U.S. Senate, went to court then to block monitors from getting inside polling and counting locations.

"The DOJ knows it has no authority to monitor Texas elections and backed down when Texas stood up for the rule of law," Paxton said in a statement on Nov. 5, 2024.

item.title: Poll: Voters want Congress to be a check on Trump, trust Democrats more on issues
item.description: Voters have record low trust in Republicans' ability to handle their top issues like immigration and rising prices, according to the latest Strength In Numbers/Verasight poll shared with NPR. The poll also finds a strong majority of voters want the next Congress to undo President Trump's agenda — or act as a check on his power — on policies like tariffs and trade, health care and immigration.
item.content:encoded:
Voters have record low trust in Republicans' ability to handle their top issues like immigration and rising prices, according to the latest Strength In Numbers/Verasight poll shared with NPR.

The poll also finds a strong majority of voters want the next Congress to undo President Trump's agenda — or act as a check on his power — on policies like tariffs and trade, health care and immigration.

Less than two weeks out from Election Day, voters say they'd prefer to elect a Democrat to Congress over a Republican by a double-digit margin among registered voters (52% to 41%) and likely voters (54% to 42%).

The survey of 2,028 respondents was conducted Oct. 13-19 and has a margin of sampling error of 2.2 percentage points, meaning results could be about 2.2 points higher or lower.

Trump's job approval sits at near-record lows for his second term, with just 34% approving of his performance and 62% disapproving, with 50% strongly disapproving.

G. Elliott Morris, author of the Strength In Numbers newsletter and CEO of polling company Wave Polling and Research, said the latest poll explains the current challenges with the political landscape Republicans face.

"Trump's ratings hit new lows on seven of the 10 issues we've tracked since May 2025, from jobs and trade to immigration and border security, and he's now underwater on every issue we ask about," Morris said. "The president's policies have even harmed Republicans, with voters now more likely to say they trust Democrats to handle the issues of immigration and the economy."

Among adults, prices and inflation are collectively mentioned far and away as the most important problem facing the country today, with 63% of respondents saying it was one of their top three most important problems and 39% listing it first. Other top issues include jobs and the economy, health care, elections and democracy and immigration.

Taken all together, the sentiment of the electorate explains why Democrats and Republicans are spending big in House and Senate races stretching deep into conservative territory where Trump performed well in 2024.

Voters chose to give Republicans control of the White House and Congress in the 2024 election, and at least some of them say they regret their choice. According to the poll, nearly one in 10 people who said they voted in the 2024 presidential race regret their choice, including almost 15% of self-described Trump voters and 15% who backed a third-party candidate.

In May 2025, the Strength in Numbers/Verasight poll found voters trusted Republicans more than Democrats on immigration and deportations by an average of 15 points. Now, they trust Democrats by a narrow one point margin.

In every measure that the poll has tracked, Republicans have lost ground in the last year and a half, and only hold a slim advantage on crime and public safety issues and border security.

When asked which party voters trust to handle their personal top issue, Democrats hold a 47-35 advantage, a nearly 10-point jump since May 2025 and the widest gap measured.

Many polls, including the September NPR/PBS News/Marist survey , find that the 2026 midterm choices are best viewed in relation to Trump rather than a pure binary vote of support for the Democratic or Republican candidates.

Only 25% of respondents said it was more important to elect a Congress that will help Trump pass his agenda, compared to 58% who said it was about electing a Congress to act as a check and balance on Trump.

Two of every five voters surveyed said their decision would mostly be a statement against Trump and his agenda, compared to one in five who said it would be a statement of support. For 20% of voters surveyed, their choice would be about specific issues and candidates in their district.

On the issues of tariffs and trade, health care, foreign policy, elections and voting, government spending and social programs, immigration and deportations and artificial intelligence, a majority of those surveyed want a Congress to roll back or act as a check on Trump's stances.

More voters think the Democratic Party cares more about people like them than Republicans, and 20% say neither party does.

item.title: Meet the people moving north to escape increasingly hot summers
item.description: Updated October 22, 2026 at 8:48 AM ChST LONDON – Mike Coe never thought he would leave his dream home in rural Worcestershire, not far from Stratford-upon-Avon, Shakespeare's birthplace.
item.content:encoded:
Updated October 22, 2026 at 8:48 AM ChST

LONDON – Mike Coe never thought he would leave his dream home in rural Worcestershire, not far from Stratford-upon-Avon, Shakespeare's birthplace.

That was until Coe started researching the warming temperatures in the region. Coe had a job making videos for environmental activists, and ten years ago, when he spoke to his colleagues about the effects of climate change – and read the scientific papers himself – he started to get concerned.

"I realized that it was likely to get very, very hot in the British Midlands, even during my lifetime," Coe, 69, told NPR. "I said… I think we need to move to Scotland." A decade later, now Coe and his partner Lizzie Stoodley live on the Isle of Skye off Scotland's west coast.

There they have built a "Passivhaus" — a highly energy-efficient home — the second they have built. And they are glad they built their new home where they did. "Our decision to move seems to have been confirmed as being the right one, particularly this year," Coe told NPR.

Friends who still live further south have told the couple that the weather was "unbelievably hot" and "incredibly uncomfortable" this summer, as the United Kingdom experienced its hottest summer on record, with five successive heat waves and widespread drought.

But while southern regions warmed up, the weather on the Isle of Skye remained temperate. "I think there are quite a few more very hot summers I might escape by living here rather than remaining where we did," Coe said.

Susan Chinnery and her partner Steve Lewis, used to live near Milton Keynes, 50 miles north of London. But they began finding the summer months increasingly uncomfortable.

"I hate the hot weather," Chinnery told NPR. "I remember 2022 when Steve and I… we were actually sleeping outside on the patio because it was just too hot to sleep indoors." Like many British homes, their Victorian-era house was designed to keep in the warmth, and doesn't have air conditioning.

Lewis said that 2022 reminded him of the famously hot British summer of 1976, and he realised it was only going to get warmer. "I thought to myself, it's arrived," he told NPR. "This is the slow and inexorable decline into some new state."

Last year, Chinnery and Lewis moved to Westray, one of the Orkney Islands off northern Scotland, largely because of rising temperatures.

Melissa Terras also moved to Scotland, partly because of climate change. "When I mentioned climate change to people as one of the reasons why we were going to move north, people laughed," Terras told NPR. "They were like, 'What are you talking about?'"

In 2017, Terras moved her family from Letchworth Garden City, a town 40 miles north of London, to Edinburgh. A professor at the University of Edinburgh, Terras chose a house "up a hill," mindful of rising sea levels. She says more people are now thinking as she did several years ago.

The trend is also emerging in the housing market. Real estate agents in the Scottish Highlands told NPR that more buyers are citing cooler summers as a factor in their home-buying decisions. Recent figures show that house prices in Scotland rose year over year, while they fell in southeastern England and Greater London.

All over Europe, there are signs that climate is beginning to influence where many people are choosing to live, alongside factors including jobs, housing and the economy.

Scientists say Europe is the world's fastest warming continent. Large areas of Europe saw scorching temperatures this summer, with widespread wildfires, and at least 35,000 excess deaths thought to have been linked to the heat.

As climate change intensifies, countries around the world are grappling with more extreme impacts. At this year's U.N. General Assembly, Nepal's prime minister, Balendra Shah, called recent flash floods in his country "a warning to the world," urging a "culture of preparedness" for future climate crises.

Gaia Vince, a London-based journalist and author of Nomad Century , predicts climate change will drive hundreds of millions of people from hotter regions to more temperate areas this century.

The U.K. has felt the effects, too. "We've had five almost consecutive heat waves this year alone, and our infrastructure is built for a completely different climate — everything is built for a climate which no longer exists," Vince told NPR.

Britain will also see migration, Vince said, as people adapt their lifestyles and infrastructure. Wealthier individuals are already moving toward places such as Ireland and Scotland in search of a more livable climate, she said.

Vince expects a similar trend in the United States, with the Great Lakes region and Alaska potentially attracting people from farther south.

Some Americans are already making the move to Scotland. Jason Sorensen, a California native, moved with his wife, Christine, last year to Golspie in the Scottish Highlands.

After experiencing wildfires in Los Angeles and hot summers while working in London, Sorensen said "something broke" inside him, and he decided he wanted to live somewhere cooler.

"Between now and 2100, there really are only a few places that you could categorize as 'best of the worst' oases if things really go to hell," Sorensen told NPR. "Certain parts of Norway, the South Island of New Zealand, maybe southern Chile down near the Lake District, maybe certain parts of Alaska — and northern Scotland."

Not so long ago, people who said they wanted to live in Scotland for the weather would have been laughed at.

But for many living farther south, it seems the joke isn't quite so funny anymore.
